papers.title: Optical clocks at sea
papers.region: US; New Zealand ship; TTCP UK relevance
papers.contribution: Integrated iodine-vapour optical clock and microwave frequency-comb output; field timing experiment [S10 Main; Methods].
papers.method: Three clock comparison at NIST against ST05/AT1, then co-located shipboard pairwise comparisons; three-cornered-hat extraction at short times, long-time equal-contribution upper bound [S10 Figs.1–3; Methods Clock comparison].
papers.result: 35 L physics/comb/control package, 26 kg, ~85 W excluding external supply. PICKLES–EPIC pair at sea: 8×10^-15 instability at 100,000 s (~400 ps equivalent daily holdover), without drift correction [S10 Fig.3d; Main].
papers.limitations: Air-conditioned shipping container; no independent high-performance reference at sea; potential correlated environmental noise acknowledged. Individual long-time bound assumes equal contributions. VIPER external supply restarted; raw versus dedrifted laboratory results differ [S10 Main; Methods; Extended Data Fig.4].
papers.replication: Different clock ensemble at same RIMPAC campaign supplies architecture-level corroboration, not independent replication of this instrument [S11 Maritime demonstration; S10 Fig.3].
papers.data_code: Raw/processed data on request; analysis routines on reasonable request, not a public archive [S10 Data availability; Code availability].
papers.conflicts: Authors declare no competing interests, but author affiliations include Vector Atomic; commercial participation must remain visible [S10 Author information; Competing interests].
papers.relevance: Analysis: credible local timing holdover evidence; no GNSS-free position solution or deployable network is measured [S10 Figs.1–3].
papers.assessment: Analysis: credible local timing holdover evidence; no GNSS-free position solution or deployable network is measured [S10 Figs.1–3].

claims.text: 35 L clock package excludes external power supply; ~85 W and 26 kg.
At sea PICKLES–EPIC pair instability is 8×10^-15 at 100,000 s, reported equivalent holdover ~400 ps/24 h without drift correction.
Long-time single-clock upper bound divides pair performance by sqrt(2), assuming equal contributions.
No independent standard reference was available at sea; correlated environmental sensitivities are acknowledged.

papers.title: Demonstration of a mobile optical clock ensemble at sea
papers.contribution: Field comparison of three distinct vapour optical architectures (Yb, two-colour Rb, single-colour Rb) [S11 Results Portable optical clocks].
papers.method: Optical/RF/microwave beats; 5071A counter timebase; three-cornered-hat Modified Allan deviations. Comparison separates reference/counter artefacts from optical instability [S11 Figs.2,4–6; Methods Clock comparisons and analysis].
papers.result: Yb ModADEV remains in 10^-14 domain from 100 ms to 80 ks; short-time (<100 s) sea performance similar to shore, but longer-time stability deteriorates [S11 Individual clock stabilities; Fig.6].
papers.limitations: Total ORAFS deployed support apparatus: 46 rack units, 310 kg, 1300 W; internal 112 L/30 kg/300 W is not complete installed system. Power interruption required manual ORAFS restart; UofA clocks restarted autonomously. Rb relocks/configuration changes produce frequency steps [S11 Fig.3; Methods Optical rubidium atomic frequency standard].
papers.replication: Independent clock designs corroborate vapour-clock ruggedness; same 2022 exercise as S10, not independent environmental campaign [S11 Maritime demonstration].
papers.data_code: Data restricted by military exercise: requests require author and sponsor approval. Processing code on reasonable request [S11 Data availability; Code availability].
papers.conflicts: Andre Luiten co-founder, owner and managing director of QuantX; company has commercial IP rights to UofA clocks. Others declare none [S11 Competing interests].
papers.relevance: Analysis: valuable comparison with practical failure/restart behaviour; read superiority as stability and application-specific SWaP, not blanket accuracy [S11 Figs.3,6,7; Table1].
papers.assessment: Analysis: valuable comparison with practical failure/restart behaviour; read superiority as stability and application-specific SWaP, not blanket accuracy [S11 Figs.3,6,7; Table1].

claims.text: Yb stability is in the 10^-14 domain from 100 ms to 80 ks.
Underway short-time clock performance resembles shore performance, but times above 100 s show decreased stability.
ORAFS deployed ancillary system totals 310 kg and 1300 W.
claims.locator: Methods Optical rubidium atomic frequency standard—ORAFS; Table1

claims.text: Power interruption required personnel to restart ORAFS; UofA systems recovered automatically.

papers.title: Atom interferometry at arbitrary orientations and rotation rates
papers.version: Journal HTML, version of record; preprint v1 also inspected
papers.contribution: Combines atomic/classical sensing and actively steered mirror to retain interferometer contrast during rotations [S12 Results; Fig.3].
papers.method: 87Rb Raman Mach–Zehnder, classical mirror accelerometer and two FOGs, manually rotated platform. Acceleration phase is servo-cancelled; rotational phase reconstructed with inertial model [S12 Results; Methods Closed-loop mode].
papers.result: 24 micro-g per-shot inferred sensitivity at 2T=20 ms; tilt 0–30 degrees, rotation up to 14 deg/s. Fringe SNR 5.3 versus 20–30 static [S12 Fig.3; Results Rotation compensation].
papers.limitations: One measurement axis and manual platform; 1.3% fitted mirror-rate correction; vibration compensation uses assumed flat accelerometer response and 610 microsecond delay. Uncharacterized classical sensor response and platform resonances degrade SNR. Full triad/long-term stability remains future work [S12 Methods; Discussion].
papers.replication: Single-instrument study with model/data agreement; no independently reproduced full navigation solution [S12 Figs.2–4; Discussion].
papers.data_code: Raw data deposited at Zenodo 11543715; analysis code release not stated in journal Data availability [S12 Data availability].
papers.conflicts: Four authors employed by Exail, which commercializes atom-interferometric gravimeters; other authors declare none [S12 Competing interests].
papers.relevance: Analysis: enabling motion-compensation result, not field navigation accuracy or classical-free autonomy [S12 Results; Discussion].
papers.assessment: Analysis: enabling motion-compensation result, not field navigation accuracy or classical-free autonomy [S12 Results; Discussion].

claims.text: Reconstructed fringe SNR 5.3 corresponds to 24 micro-g per shot at 20 ms interrogation.
Experiment reaches tilts 0–30 degrees and rotation rates up to 14 degrees/s on a manual rotation platform.
Mirror-rate reconstruction uses fitted correction epsilon=-0.013.
claims.locator: Results Rotation compensation; Methods Correction of phase shift

claims.text: Vibration compensation assumes constant accelerometer response and global 610-microsecond delay.
claims.locator: Methods Limits of fringe reconstruction due to strong vibrations

papers.title: Quantum-assured magnetic navigation achieves positioning accuracy better than a strategic-grade INS in airborne and ground-based field trials
papers.version: arXiv 2504.08167v1 HTML; no journal reference on inspected landing page
papers.contribution: Field magnetic-map navigation with internally mounted rubidium scalar magnetometer, vector fluxgate, INS and adaptive compensation [S13 System architecture; Field trials].
papers.method: Griffith Cessna flights February 2025 (>6700 km recorded) and van trials November 2024; causal iterative filter described, online warm/cold platform learning; public Australian TMI maps, INS aided by scalar airspeed or 3D velocity [S13 Q-CTRL magnetic denoising; Field trials; Table1].
papers.result: 22 m endpoint is 365 km, onboard sensor plus 3D velocity aiding (15× INS). 46× example uses outboard sensor and 3D velocity (112 m endpoint). Strict-denial onboard/airspeed case 515 m on 365 km; high-altitude onboard case 2 km/300 km; ground 180 m/18 km [S13 Table1; Figs.4–7].
papers.limitations: No same-map algorithm comparison or classical scalar magnetometer ablation. 3D velocity provenance not specified sufficiently for strict GNSS-free best-case interpretation. Algorithms proprietary; altitude extension, military dynamics, ocean coverage remain unresolved [S13 Fig.1 caption; System architecture; Table1; Discussion].
papers.replication: No independent replication identified in bounded search; authors use outboard sensors for within-study checks [S13 Field trials; Fig.5].
papers.data_code: No explicit data/code availability statement found in inspected full v1; proprietary magnetometer and software descriptions prevent reconstruction from text alone [S13 Q-CTRL MagNav System; end matter inspected].
papers.conflicts: All authors affiliated Q-CTRL; proprietary/commercial full-stack system. No separate conflicts declaration found in inspected v1 [S13 author list; Q-CTRL MagNav System].
papers.relevance: Analysis: credible internally mounted field aid, but advantage is over specified INS, not GPS and not isolated quantum-sensor advantage [S13 Table1; Demonstration of MagNav].
papers.assessment: Analysis: credible internally mounted field aid, but advantage is over specified INS, not GPS and not isolated quantum-sensor advantage [S13 Table1; Demonstration of MagNav].

claims.text: 22 m endpoint uses onboard sensor with 3D-velocity aid over 365 km.
46× endpoint improvement uses outboard sensor with 3D velocity; endpoint112 m.
Onboard scalar-airspeed example ends at515 m over365 km; high-altitude onboard example ends at2 km over300 km.
Algorithms and scalar sensor are proprietary; public text gives no same-input classical scalar-sensor ablation.
claims.locator: Q-CTRL MagNav System; Demonstration of MagNav; full v1 inspected

papers.title: GNSS-free quantum gravity-aided navigation and fine-scale marine surveying with a strapdown quantum gravimeter
papers.version: arXiv 2608.25563v1 HTML; no journal reference on inspected landing page
papers.region: Australia; trial funded by UK Royal Navy/DASA
papers.contribution: Maritime quantum-gravity map aiding with explicit exclusion of GNSS from processing; separate gravity-survey branch [S14 Results Quantum navigation; Methods Gravity-aided navigation].
papers.method: 87Rb Mach–Zehnder plus mirror accelerometer bias stabilization; recorded raw Boreas D90 IMU independently mechanized; error-state filter combines gravity map and position/velocity/attitude/bias estimates over 83 km southbound route [S14 Fig.6; Methods Quantum–classical hybridization; Gravity-aided navigation].
papers.result: Endpoint 2.2 nmi (~4.1 km), versus unaided 14 nmi (~26 km); ~1 nmi for first 70 km. GNSS-referenced strapdown survey separately reports 0.67 mGal in-run stability and 0.16 mGal repeatability. Stationary 56 h hybrid stability ~70× classical at 80,000 s [S14 Fig.2; Figs.4,7; Methods].
papers.limitations: Initial state only described as same for both branches; provenance/uncertainty not specified. Fully closed long-duration campaign future work; onboard real-time execution not established. Coastal strapdown typically Sea State1 versus gimbaled2–3, so not matched-motion equality. 30 L sensor head excludes electronics rack [S14 Results; Methods Maritime traversals; Quantum sensor head; Discussion]. Internal wording inconsistency: abstract invokes nautical-mile DRMS, Fig.2 says shaded one-mile band is not DRMS, Discussion suggests ~one-mile bound, while Results/Methods report 2.2-nmi endpoint. Do not infer a universal one-mile bound or computed DRMS [S14 Abstract; Fig.2 caption; Results Quantum navigation; Discussion].
papers.replication: Within-instrument comparisons, no independent replication identified. Survey data expressly supply no observations to GNSS-free route; GNSS remains ground truth and survey PVA/Eötvös source [S14 Methods Gravity signal for surveying; Gravity-aided navigation].
papers.data_code: No explicit data/code release statement found in v1 full text/end matter. Filter is described structurally, without sufficient full tuning/implementation for reproduction [S14 Methods; Acknowledgments/end matter inspected].
papers.conflicts: Q-CTRL-funded/developed commercial participation; Royal Navy/DASA support acknowledged. No separate conflict statement found in inspected v1 [S14 author affiliations; Acknowledgments].
papers.relevance: Analysis: recent provisional evidence of complete processing-chain GNSS exclusion, not centimetric navigation, multiday endurance or survey performance in denial [S14 Fig.2; Methods; Discussion].
papers.assessment: Analysis: recent provisional evidence of complete processing-chain GNSS exclusion, not centimetric navigation, multiday endurance or survey performance in denial [S14 Fig.2; Methods; Discussion].

claims.text: 83 km evaluated route ends at2.2 nmi (~4.1km), compared with14 nmi (~26km) unaided.
claims.locator: Results Quantum navigation with gravity map matching; Fig.2

claims.text: Methods explicitly exclude embedded Boreas GNSS-derived position/velocity/attitude from navigation mechanization.
Separate surveying branch uses GNSS-disciplined PVA for rotation, Eotvos correction and georeferencing.
claims.locator: Methods Gravity signal for surveying and anomaly detection; Fig.8

claims.text: Coastal strapdown traversals typically experienced Sea State1 versus gimbaled Sea States2–3.
claims.locator: Methods Maritime and land traversal details

papers.title: Integration of a high-fidelity model of quantum sensors with a map-matching filter for quantum-enhanced navigation
papers.version: arXiv 2504.11119v2 (8 August 2025); published QST 10 045007; journal metadata via Crossref
papers.contribution: Microscopic sensor simulation linked to navigation filter; important adverse result: non-Gaussian motion errors can make nominal sensitivity improvements unusable [S15 §§II–V].
papers.method: Monte-Carlo atomic cloud/internal–external trajectory/pulse model; maritime/aircraft trajectories, moderate/enhanced/mitigated sensor capabilities, particle map-matching filter and classical INS model [S15 §II.2; §III; §IV; App.C].
papers.result: Sea State2 moderate/enhanced cases could not be tuned to useful stable aiding; mitigation uses 5× reduced roll/pitch. Flight cases require assumed 100× motion reduction for bounded estimates. Static tilt <3.3 degrees derived for 10 E error budget [S15 §IV; Figs.7–8; App.B.1].
papers.limitations: Simulation, not field navigation. All runs have 30 s transfer alignment, 100 m north/east initial errors; particle weighting tuned to observed sensor noise and maritime sea-state segments. Mitigation assumed, not experimentally delivered [S15 §IV; App.C; §V].
papers.replication: Model checks and conditional simulations, not independent field replication. Tests against measured complete dynamic sensor/nav chain still needed (Analysis) [S15 §II.2; §IV; §V].
papers.data_code: All supporting data/code available on reasonable request to corresponding author; no archive link in statement [S15 Data availability statement].
papers.conflicts: Authors declare no competing interests [S15 Competing Interests].
papers.relevance: Analysis: strengthens assessment by specifying where optimistic navigation simulations fail; 3.3-degree bound is conditional, not a universal navigation tolerance [S15 App.B; §IV].
papers.assessment: Analysis: strengthens assessment by specifying where optimistic navigation simulations fail; 3.3-degree bound is conditional, not a universal navigation tolerance [S15 App.B; §IV]. Confidence high in reported conditional simulation result, medium in physical-model fidelity outside validated conditions; not an experiment.

claims.text: Moderate/enhanced Sea State2 simulated measurements could not be tuned to useful stable aiding.
Successful high-dynamic flight aiding assumes100-fold reduced roll/pitch.
3.3-degree static tilt requirement follows a specified10 E error budget, not universal accuracy tolerance.
Runs start with30 s transfer alignment and assumed100 m north/east initialization errors.
claims.locator: §IV Integration with a map-matching navigation filter
